content: Bipolar disorder is a serious and prevalent mental health condition characterized by recurring episodes of elevated or irritable mood, depression, or a combination of both. Treatment typically involves psychiatric medications, including mood stabilizers, antidepressants, and antipsychotics. Valproate is recognized as an effective maintenance therapy for bipolar disorder, but its efficacy in treating acute manic episodes is less well-established, particularly in comparison to newer antipsychotic medications. This review updates a previous Cochrane Review from 2003, focusing on the role of valproate in managing acute mania. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of valproate for treating acute manic episodes in bipolar disorder. This was assessed by measuring symptom improvement using specific rating scales in pediatric, adolescent, and adult populations. Comparisons were made between valproate and placebo, alternative pharmacological treatments, or combination therapies. The search strategy included databases such as Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, with the most recent search conducted in September 2018. Additional searches were performed in the World Health Organization trials portal and clinicaltrials.gov to identify unpublished or ongoing studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (both singleand double-blind) that compared valproate with placebo, other antimanic treatments, or combination therapies. Studies involving valproate as an adjunctive treatment were analyzed separately from those where it was used as monotherapy. Participants included males and females of all ages and ethnicities diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Data extraction and quality assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers. For binary efficacy outcomes, odds ratios (OR) were used, while mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) were applied for continuous outcomes. The review analyzed 25 trials involving 3,252 participants, comparing valproate with placebo or alternative antimanic treatments for alleviating acute manic symptoms. The primary efficacy outcome was the response rate, while the primary tolerability outcome was the proportion of participants experiencing adverse effects. The studies included children, adolescents, and adults with varying severities of manic symptoms. Most studies focused on adults (aged 18 and above) in inpatient settings, primarily conducted in the United States. Five studies included children and adolescents (aged 18 and under), covering an age range of 3 to 82 years. Seven studies involved outpatient participants, and nine studies were conducted outside the US, including in Iran, India, China, and international settings. In adults, high-quality evidence demonstrated that valproate was slightly more effective than placebo in inducing a response (45% vs. 29%; OR 2.05, 95% CI 1.32 to 3.20; 4 studies, 869 participants). Moderate-quality evidence suggested little or no difference in response rates between valproate and lithium (56% vs. 62%; OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.35; 3 studies, 356 participants). Low-quality evidence indicated that there might be little or no difference in response rates between valproate and olanzapine (38% vs. 44%; OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.25; 2 studies, 667 participants). In children and adolescents, the evidence regarding differences in response rates between valproate and placebo was uncertain (23% vs. 22%; OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.51 to 2.38; 1 study, 151 participants, very low-quality evidence). Low-quality evidence suggested that valproate might be less effective than risperidone in this population (23% vs. 66%; OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.29; 1 study, 197 participants). The evidence comparing valproate and lithium in children and adolescents was also uncertain (23% vs. 34%; OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.07; 1 study, 197 participants, very low-quality evidence). Regarding tolerability in adults, moderate-quality evidence indicated that valproate was associated with a higher likelihood of adverse events compared to placebo (83% vs. 75%; OR 1.63, 95% CI 1.13 to 2.36; 3 studies, 745 participants). Low-quality evidence suggested little or no difference in tolerability between valproate and lithium (78% vs. 86%; OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.50; 2 studies, 164 participants). No primary tolerability data were available for the comparison between valproate and olanzapine. In children and adolescents, the evidence regarding tolerability differences between valproate and placebo was uncertain (67% vs. 60%; OR 1.39, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.71; 1 study, 150 participants, very low-quality evidence). No primary tolerability data were available for comparisons between valproate and lithium or risperidone. In conclusion, valproate appears to be an effective treatment for acute mania in adults when compared to placebo. However, there is no evidence to suggest a difference in efficacy between valproate and placebo in children and adolescents. Valproate may be less effective than olanzapine in adults and potentially inferior to risperidone as a monotherapy for pediatric mania. The evidence regarding the side effect profile of valproate compared to other antimanic therapies remains uncertain, though it may cause less weight gain and sedation than olanzapine.
